title: Exercise behavior of ultramarathon runners: baseline findings from the ULTRA study
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: Current and former ultramarathon runners in the Ultrarunners Longitudinal TRAcking (ULTRA) Study, baseline data
findings: Exercise history collected on 1,345 current and former ultramarathon runners; 1,212 were active.

Median age at first ultramarathon was 36 years; median years of regular running before the first ultramarathon was 7 (IQR 3-15); years of regular running before the first ultra fell with calendar year (r = -0.13, p < 0.0001).

Active runners had a previous-year median running distance of 3,347 km (about 64 km/week, derived by dividing by 52), minimally related to age (r = -0.068, p = 0.018) but mostly related to their longest ultramarathon of the year (p < 0.0001).
25% had been regularly running for 3 years or less at the time of their first ultramarathon.
Running injuries were the most common reason for discontinuing regular running; work and family commitments were the main reasons for not running an ultramarathon in the prior year.
limitations: Self-reported, retrospective, convenience cohort of mostly US ultrarunners; describes habits, not predictors of outcome; the median is for experienced, active ultrarunners and is not a prescription.
implications: Use about 64 km/week (3,347 km/yr median) only as a descriptive benchmark to sanity-check a recreational athlete's peak volume; never as a target.

Show an informational note when the athlete has under 3 years of regular running before a first ultra: this is the lower quarter of the observed distribution. The paper does not show that this group is at higher risk; the risk direction comes from [sewry-2022-safer-xxi-dnf] and [hoffman-2014-ultra-health-injury].
Keep an explicit injury-load check in the progression logic because injury is the most common reason ultrarunners stop regular running.

verification.notes: Crossref (2013-11, first author Hoffman; Crossref omits the subtitle) and Europe PMC abstract re-fetched. Removed the unsupported claim that the under-3-years group is injury-prone. The task text said 2014; this paper is 2013, the 2014 ULTRA paper is added separately.
